data.title: Prime Video releases trailer for 2-part Melania Trump series
data.description:
Prime Video announced the release of a two-part series on First Lady Melania Trump’s life since her husband returned to office, unveiling a trailer for the new feature on Friday.

The series, titled “MELANIA, The Series,” offers new insight into the behind-the-scenes life of the first lady.

“The Series reveals never-before-told stories, offering unprecedented insight into Melania Trump’s life, including the extraordinary days immediately following the 47th Presidential Inauguration,” Prime Video said.

The first episode, titled “Family & Trust,” will focus on her setting priorities ahead of her return to the White House, and the second episode, titled “Pride & Honor,” focuses on setting “her mission in motion.”

The new series follows Amazon’s release of the “Melania” movie, a documentary film on the 20 days leading up to President Trump’s inauguration.

Amazon spent $75 million on the film to acquire and market its release, but it only made $16 million at the box office. Melania Trump was an executive producer on the film.

At the time, some Democratic lawmakers, including Rep. Hank Johnson (D-Ga.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said they would investigate whether the movie’s release was a “pay-to-play scheme,” arguing Amazon has several financial interests in the hands of the Trump administration.

Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos attended Trump’s inauguration and has had a cozier relationship with Trump during his second term in office. Still, after the film’s release, Bezos denied having anything to do with the decision to acquire it. 

“Amazon’s a big company and makes a lot of decisions. But no, this idea that somehow that is a way of buying influence, it’s just not. It’s just not correct,” Bezos said at the time.

The new two-part series will begin streaming Nov. 20 on Prime Video.

data.title: How Scott Colom turned his Mississippi Senate race into a nailbiter
data.description:
Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) is fighting for her political life as Democrat Scott Colom threatens to pull off one of the biggest upsets of the midterms in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1982.

Before polls closed on Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave Hyde-Smith a 91 percent chance of winning her race. But by late Friday afternoon, Colom led by 2,734 votes in DDHQ’s tally, with thousands of ballots still outstanding. 

Some of Colom’s biggest gains have come in counties Hyde-Smith won handily six years ago. In the Memphis suburbs, he leads by roughly 6 points in DeSoto County, which she carried by 16 points in 2020. On the Gulf Coast, the incumbent’s lead in Harrison County has narrowed from 17 points in 2020 to about 4 points in the latest unofficial count. 

Colom has also picked up votes in places where Republicans still led by wide margins. In Pearl River County, Colom drew about 4,000 votes, or 24 percent, in the preliminary count — compared to the 2,400 votes, or 22 percent, that Democratic gubernatorial nominee Brandon Presley got in 2023. Former Vice President Harris won 16 percent of the vote in 2024.

Colom benefited from a national political environment that favored Democrats, but he also gave voters in Mississippi a local target for their frustration over rising prices by turning Hyde-Smith’s suggestion that shoppers choose a cheaper protein into a pitch to “pick another senator.”

Organizers worked to turn out Black voters, and preliminary returns show about 10 percent more votes were cast in majority-Black counties than in the 2023 governor’s race. The New York Times estimated that 91 percent of Black voters back Colom.

The Times’s preliminary estimates show a shift toward Democrats across age, race, gender and education groups compared to 2024. Hyde-Smith still led among white voters by 49 points, but that was 19 points narrower than President Trump’s margin with those voters two years earlier.

New Southern Majority, a super PAC launched by the Southern Poverty Law Center’s political advocacy arm, saw an opening to reach GOP voters while other organizations focused on turning out Black voters this cycle, according to Brannon Miller, whose consulting firm, Chism Strategies, ran the effort. 

He said the group spent just under $1 million on messaging to Republican voters in the race, targeting about 200,000 Republicans with messages that focused almost entirely on criticizing Hyde-Smith over issues including the war in Iran, high gas prices, tariffs and her support for data centers. 

Miller suggested that messaging was effective, pointing to Colom’s gains in red counties like Pearl River and DeSoto as a sign that some voters who typically back Republicans crossed over this cycle.

“There’s literally no other explanation,” Miller said. “These are places where Democrats get less than 15 percent of the vote in a presidential year. There are not Democrats there to turn out.”

“So when Scott Colom doubles the number of votes that Brandon Presley got in some of these counties, or close to it, that has to be coming from white Republicans flipping and voting for the first black senator since Reconstruction,” he continued. 

DeSoto stands out as the county that saw the biggest swing toward Democrats from the 2024 presidential race. Trump carried the fast-growing Memphis suburbs by 24 points in 2024, but Colom is now leading by roughly 6 points, accounting for a 30-point shift over just two years. Colom drew about 28,100 votes in the county, nearly twice as many as Presley received there in 2023. 

“In my mind, a big part of the swing is explained by the opposition to data centers,” Miller said, pointing to a facility in DeSoto that has drawn significant backlash from locals about persistent noise issues.

DeSoto County Democratic Party Chair Deborah Williams said she also thought the backlash to the data center might have hurt Hyde-Smith’s support, but she attributed more of the swing to the work organizers did, knocking on nearly 70,000 doors and working to increase absentee ballots.

She also said she thinks voters weren’t excited about Hyde-Smith and that Colom’s “Mississippi Matters” message resonated especially with young voters. On Election Day, she said she went from precinct to precinct and was surprised to see just how many young voters were lining up at the polls. She said some were waiting two or three hours in the rain just to get a chance to vote.

“[Mississippi] had been perceived as a deep-red state, but it really wasn’t a deep-red state. It was a state where people weren’t engaged in this process for a number of different reasons,” Williams said. “So yes, I think Scott had a lot to do with bringing that sense of pride back to the state of Mississippi, and people did embrace that.”

Arekia Bennett-Scott, executive director of Mississippi Votes, said young people have been organizing in the state for years but the push to redraw Mississippi’s congressional districts gave them a particular reason to show up this year.

Bennett-Scott noted that many students saw redistricting as a threat to Black political representation and responded by rallying in Jackson in May and organizing across campuses.

“They understand that voting is a tool, not the only tool, but it’s a tool that they can fight back with this particular election cycle,” she said, referring to youth turnout. 

The Times estimated that voters under 30 in Mississippi backed Colom, 62 percent to 33 percent — a whopping 44-point swing toward Democrats compared to 2024. 

But the political organizer emphasized that the higher youth engagement is not about any single candidate or party.

“Young people are fighting towards power, and that speaks to the way that they showed up,” Bennett-Scott said, adding, “They know what’s at stake, and they align themselves with what and who was speaking the language of justice for them in this moment.”

The razor-thin margins in the deep-red Mississippi Senate race took many political observers by surprise, but local organizers note that the state has gotten a lot more competitive in recent years and people are only now paying attention. 

“I think that there’s a stereotype of the state as being what it was in the 1960s that just no longer holds,” Miller said. 

“It’s not like this is a new Mississippi,” he continued. “This is the Mississippi that’s been there for at least the past decade. This was just finally when all of the right confluence of circumstances came together to allow us to win.”

data.title: Houston mayor looks to limit city's cooperation with ICE after Democrats' wins in Texas
data.description:
Houston Mayor John Whitmire (D) said the city would limit cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents just days after Democrats swept the state-level offices in the midterm elections.

The mayor said his executive order applied to nonviolent criminals, who will be released with a citation, and that unless someone is arrested for an offense, ICE will not be notified even if they have an outstanding immigration warrant.

“I do this to begin a healing process, reduce fear and anxiety across our community,” Whitmire said at a news conference on Friday. 

Houston has been at the center of multiple confrontations with ICE agents this year, including, most recently, the indictment of an ICE agent who prosecutors say struck an undocumented Mexican immigrant with his vehicle. 

Back in July, ICE agents in Houston fatally shot a Mexican man who had lived in the U.S. for 35 years. Some in Texas left “I Voted” stickers on his memorial ahead of the election.

Houston previously passed an ordinance to limit police cooperation with federal immigration agents, but Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) opened an investigation into the move, accusing it of violating Texas Senate Bill 4, a law that prevents cities from taking up policies to limit immigration enforcement. 

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) then threatened to hold up $110 million in public safety funding unless the ordinance was repealed, which it ultimately was.

Paxton was already set to leave the attorney general’s office, opting to run for Senate instead. He was defeated on Tuesday by state Rep. James Talarico (D) by 12 points. The Republican running to replace Paxton lost too.

Abbott lost his seat in the governor’s mansion to state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D). The Democrats’ statewide sweep marks a major shift in the Lone Star State’s political power.

Whitmire acknowledged that the election played a role in the policy change.

“I also do this knowing elections matter,” Whitmire said. “I’ve been in contact with the new statewide elected officials, and SB 4 is not a priority of the new statewide elected officials.”

As governor, Abbott spent billions on border security when President Joe Biden was in office. Hinojosa has previously called the Texas governor’s operation “political theatre,” and said she would review the operation.

Democrats took control of the state House in Texas, but will remain in the minority in the Texas Senate, preventing them from fully undoing some GOP policies.

data.title: Acton: 'No intention' of speaking with Ramaswamy after 'beyond the pale' ad
data.description:
Gov.-elect Amy Acton (D-Ohio) said Friday that she does not plan to speak with her former opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, after he ran a controversial attack ad against her in the final weeks of the campaign.

Ramaswamy debuted an ad featuring Acton’s mother, who lost custody of her daughter when Acton was 12, which she called her daughter a “liar” and encouraged Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton’s stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her, and her mother remained with him until his death.

In a Friday interview on CBS Mornings, Acton said she did not take Ramaswamy’s concession phone call because she did not want to “normalize” his behavior.

“I think we can’t normalize behavior like this. It was so beyond the pale,” Acton told CBS News. “So no, I have no intention of speaking to him. I do believe that leaders’ words matter, and we need to hold folks accountable.”

Acton said Friday that Ramaswamy’ s use of the ad was “terrible and despicable.”

“I would like to say I didn’t expect this, but there was no low my opponent wouldn’t sink to. These ads had been full of lies and hate and vitriol the entire campaign,” Acton said.

Acton defeated Ramaswamy in the gubernatorial race by a margin of nearly 8 points Tuesday, and will be the first woman to serve as governor of Ohio.

Ramaswamy’s ad drew harsh criticism and pushback from members of both parties, including Ohio’s current governor, Mike DeWine (R), and former governor, John Kasich (R). But President Trump and Vice President Vance both defended the tactic, with Vance even saying he was “disgusted” by Republicans who criticized the ad.

In his concession speech Tuesday night, Ramaswamy struck a conciliatory tone.

“It was a tough race. It was bitter, at times, in both directions,” Ramaswamy said. “I have hope and confidence that she will do what is required to bring Ohio together.”

Acton similarly said people are “tired of the hate” and ready for “decency.”

“People are exhausted of living this way. They’re tired of the hate and chaos and vitriol,” Acton told CBS News. “Kindness isn’t weakness, and that is a big message we saw. People are ready for public service, unity, and decency.”

data.title: Watch live: Trump to speak from Kennedy Space Center days after GOP midterm losses
data.description:
President Trump is set to deliver remarks Friday at the John F. Kennedy Space Center in Florida, days after Republicans suffered sweeping losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

He is participating in NASA’s “MAX POWER” aerospace technology expo, which showcases advances in aviation, space exploration and emerging technologies. The appearance comes as the Trump administration pushes to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028, a key goal of the space agency’s Artemis program.

The president signed a proclamation on Election Day declaring that the Earth’s solar system and outer space “are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence” by U.S. citizens. 

His remarks also come hours after Trump announced he was replacing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with longtime adviser Stephen Miller.

The event is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. EST.

Watch live above.

data.title: Democrats blast 'dangerous' elevation of Miller as refusal to learn from the election
data.description:
To congressional Democrats, President Trump’s decision to promote aide Stephen Miller to serve as his chief of staff meant two things: an elevation of the aide’s extremist views and a refusal to heed the will of voters who delivered the left a historic victory.

“Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote on X shortly after Trump’s announcement.

“Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

Meanwhile, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to serve as the next Speaker, said Miller should instead be fired.

“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries said in a statement after the announcement.

“His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.”

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles resigned Thursday after Republicans’ brutal performance in the midterms, prompting Trump to turn to his longtime aide, telling reporters, “we’ve got to make some moves.” 

Miller has been the voice behind some of Trump’s most controversial policies, from the family separation policy of the president’s first term to the mass deportation operation pushed by the White House today.

“Stephen Miller is the architect of Project 2025, which included the push for ‘unitary executive power’ that Trump used to enrich himself and his billionaire buddies, enable the failed efforts of Elon Musk and DOGE, the stripping of healthcare from millions of people, and the mass deportation agenda that led to [immigration agents] killing people in the streets, separating families, locking up kids and gutting the legal immigration system,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), the head of the House Judiciary Committee subcommittee on immigration, said in a statement.

Incoming Democratic committee chairs blasted Trump’s decision to elevate Miller.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), expected to take over as chair of the House Oversight Committee, said Miller’s promotion would not stall any of their investigations into him or Trump immigration policies.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down. Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families,” Garcia said in a statement.

“Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts. Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

The reaction was particularly harsh among those who have oversight of Miller’s role as a mastermind of Trump’s immigration policies.

“Stephen Miller is a vile, hate-filled extremist who has made cruelty his life’s work,” House Homeland Security Democrats said in a statement.

“America just rejected the fear and bigotry he peddles and Trump handed him a promotion. They have learned nothing.”

Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chair Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.) referred to Tuesday’s election results as a referendum on the Trump immigration policies spearheaded by Miller.

“Just a few days ago, the American people resoundingly rejected mass deportations, the targeting of Latino communities, and President Trump’s politics of hate. To elevate the architect of those policies as White House chief of staff is a desperate and irresponsible cry for attention,” he said in a statement.

“This administration is already stained through and through with Stephen Miller’s cruelty. To give him a fancier title is just putting lipstick on a pig. Democrats were ready to expose Stephen Miller when he was hiding in the shadows and we are more than ready to expose Stephen Miller from his ill-deserved perch. Buckle up and lawyer up,” Espaillat added.

Trump Cabinet officials praised his announcement, but congressional Republicans were largely quiet.

“Our country is at a pivotal point and Stephen Miller understands exactly what is at stake. He will be an outstanding Chief of Staff,” Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), wrote on X.

“Nobody has fought harder or more effectively to secure our border and put America First. For Arizona, border security is national security. The President made an outstanding choice!” Rep. Paul Gosar (R-Ariz.) shared in a post.

But exiting Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) blamed Miller’s approach to immigration for costing the GOP the midterms, noting a swing in support from Republicans to Democrats on the topic.

“I do think [the choice] largely centers around the president likes folks who are loyal to him, his inner circle. But I just don’t think Steve Miller has much support, no support on the Democrat side, and I think he has very weak support on the Republican side,” Bacon said during an interview with ABC News.

“And I just think the president’s inner circle is living in a bubble, and they’re not hearing clearly from the American voters, but even many on the Republican side. And we’ve had meetings with Mr. Miller and his staff, and we try telling them you’re going to cost us the election in the midterms, and he didn’t believe it.”

In Democratic circles, the insults for Miller were free-flowing.

“Stephen Miller is a radical ideologue who proudly bolsters a dangerous administration’s worst impulses,” Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.) wrote on X.

“Stephen Miller has masterminded the most hateful moments of this Admin. Elevating someone defined by spite and division is a disaster for this country,” Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) wrote on the site.

“Stephen Miller is a white supremacist,” Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) said in a statement.

“Stephen Miller is the chief architect of Trump’s racist, cruel, and un-American campaign of terror across our country. Innocent people have died and families have been torn apart because of the policies he’s eagerly pushed,” Sen. Catherine Cortez-Masto (D-Nev.) wrote on X.

“The American people are begging the White House to focus on lowering costs, but the best Trump can do is ‘more Stephen Miller and the culture of cruelty,’” Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) wrote in a post.

“He just doesn’t get it.”

data.title: Bottoms taps Tyler Perry for her Georgia transition team
data.description:
Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) has tapped media mogul Tyler Perry to join her gubernatorial transition team, she announced Friday.

In an Atlanta press conference, Bottoms outlined her plans the governor’s mansion — including who would lead her transition team, which she dubbed, “Georgia’s Promise.” The governor-elect described Perry, whom she named a “co-chair” of the group, as an “entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community.”

The announcement came after the former Atlanta mayor defeated Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson in Georgia’s competitive gubernatorial race by over eight points, according to Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner.

The “Madea” creator began his entertainment career in Atlanta, and his production company, Tyler Perry Studios, is based in the city. Bottoms previously worked as an executive producer on one of Perry’s shows, Netflix’s “Miss Governor” — a political comedy which ran for one season and ended in 2025, according to film database IMDB.

Bottoms’s transition team included a lineup of prominent Georgia figures — including Home Depot co-founder Arthur Blank, former Walgreens CEO Rosalind Brewer, nonprofit leader Michelle Nunn and Delta executive Richard Cox, among others.

Election handicapper Cook Political Report had rated the race as a “toss-up” in late October. In its final rating, a day before Election Day, Sabato’s Crystal Ball changed the contest from a “toss-up” to “leans democratic.”

Bottoms will become Georgia’s first Democratic governor since Roy Barnes left office in 2003, adding to the blue wave on Election Day. Before Barnes’s departure from the governor’s mansion, Democrats had filled the Peach State’s highest office for over a century.

data.title: Jeffries calls Miller a 'dangerous xenophobe' after promotion: 'Fire him today'
data.description:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is sounding off on Stephen Miller, President Trump’s pick to replace outgoing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries said in a post to the social platform X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Miller’s promotion is not likely to be well-received by Democrats, who view the new chief of staff as inflammatory and a hardliner. Miller is a primary architect of Trump’s strict immigration enforcement agenda, having pushed some of the president’s tougher policies over the years.

Last year, Miller said the Trump administration would seek to triple its daily immigration arrests to 3,000. He said the administration was actively looking into suspending habeas corpus rights, which allow those in custody to challenge their detention. And after two American citizens were shot and killed in Minneapolis by federal immigration agents, Miller referred to the victims as domestic terrorists.

Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, is one of several Democrats who blasted the move Friday. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Trump had “learned nothing” from the results of the midterms, in which Democrats stormed back into control of both chambers of Congress.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, said Democrats would “continue to investigate” Miller.

“Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct,” Garcia said in a statement posted to X. “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Trump elevated Miller to the chief of staff role Friday, announcing in a post to Truth Social that Wiles would be leaving the role, just days after calling a report that Wiles may depart “TOTAL FAKE NEWS.”

Since Republicans’ midterm losses, some in the party, including former Trump adviser Steve Bannon, said Wiles should be fired. One former Trump aide, however, previously called the idea of Miller being chief of staff “terrifying.”

“The idea that in the last two years of Trump’s administration, when he’s going to be spiraling because he’s a lame-duck president,” former Deputy Press Secretary Sarah Matthews told MeidasTouch. “The idea of someone like a Stephen Miller in charge is a very scary thing.”

data.title: Cornell Faculty Senate passes no-confidence vote over Jane Doe case, but Board of Trustees backs president
data.description:
The Cornell Faculty Senate on Friday passed its no-confidence vote against the university administration and President Michael Kotlikoff after allegations of gang rape at a campus fraternity roiled the country. 

By 55 percent to 37 percent, with 7 percent abstaining, the symbolic vote marks the latest stage in the backlash to how the university handled accusations by Jane Doe in 2024 that she was coerced into drugs and alcohol before being sexually assaulted by seven fellow students at the Chi Phi fraternity. 

The vote has no power to remove the president or any administrators, and the Board of Trustees promptly released a statement backing Kotlikoff it. 

“Today’s Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable. There is no place for sexual violence on the Cornell campus. We support President Kotlikoff’s commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again,” Anne Smalling, chair of the university’s Board of Trustees, said in a statement.  

“The Board fully supports President Kotlikoff and his administration as they continue to listen and act decisively in support of students,” the statement concludes. 

The university has taken several steps to address the issue, including hiring an independent review of how it handled Jane Doe’s allegations and making a deal with New York for sexual assault allegations to be handled by state police.  

In an interview with The New York Times, Kotlikoff said the university has a fuller picture now of what happened than it did when the allegations were made in 2024.  

At the time, the district attorney did not pursue charges and only two of the seven men accused were expelled from Cornell.  

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) has tapped state Attorney General Letitia James to investigate the matter, with multiple members of the so-called Cornell 7 attempting to get her off the case after James posted a message in support of Jane Doe on social media before she was appointed to the case.

data.title: Christie mulling White House bid, says 'Trump era is over'
data.description:
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) is considering a White House run in 2028, telling his party to go in “a completely different direction” after sizable midterm losses.

In an interview with Politico on Wednesday, Christie said he sees himself as better positioned to run than other prominent Republicans — specifically Vice President Vance — because he has consistently criticized Trump during his second term. He called out Vance’s post blaming GOP losses on the Iran war, which Vance has publicly supported.

“The vice president to me has no credibility. He’s been sitting in the White House now for the last two years,” Christie told Politico. “[I] haven’t heard him say a negative word, you know, until this past Wednesday, and he limited it just to the war in Iran, which is not the only problem we have here.”

The two-time presidential candidate may launch a third campaign in 2028, he told Politico, saying he would make that decision “in the next few months.”

During his 2024 campaign, Christie urged the party to move on from Trump rather than nominate him again and was one of the only candidates who was willing to take on the president directly.

“The Trump era is over,” he told Politico. “We need to look forward to new leadership in our party and our country.”

After ending his campaign, Christie did not endorse a 2024 candidate.

Major midterm losses for the GOP, coupled with the president’s unpopularity, could mean that the party chooses to pivot away from Trump in the 2028 presidential primaries.

Jockeying is already underway for those primaries. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), usually a Trump ally, called the midterms a “rebuke” of the president. 

Christie also singled out DeSantis in his Politico interview, accusing him of seeking “a way to be relevant.”

“I think the governor is getting ready to leave office, and he’s looking for a way to be relevant,” Christie said. “And I think he looks like he’s talking out of both sides of his mouth.”

Other Republicans releasing election post-mortems include Sens. Ted Cruz and John Cornyn (R-Texas), who criticized their party and encouraged them to focus more on cost of living issues. Cruz and Cornyn’s home state was the site of major political upsets Tuesday as Democrats swept the statewide races. Cruz, also a previous presidential candidate, is considered a possible contender in 2028.

Candidates for the next presidential election could announce in the coming weeks or months. In 2022, Trump announced he would run again right after the midterms.
